title: Sukkot, the booth
hook: at harvest, Jews live in booths open to the sky (Leviticus 23:42)

segments.voice: Yesterday, May Day, and the hands behind a cup of coffee. Your line was thank the workers. Who did you thank by name? Today, the end of the week, and a festival where the harvest is in and everyone moves outside. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

In a backyard, on a balcony, in a parking lot behind a synagogue, someone is building a hut. Four walls, more or less. A roof of branches and leaves, laid loose on purpose, so the stars can show through. Paper chains and hanging fruit. A folding table inside, and a wobbly chair. For a week, the family will eat here, sit here, and some will sleep here, while their solid house stands empty a few steps away. The harvest is in. The barns are full. And this is where they choose to live. Today: Sukkot.
screen: `A HUT IN THE BACKYARD.` → `A ROOF YOU CAN SEE THROUGH.` → `THE HOUSE STANDS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, the command. Sukkot means booths, and the festival comes straight from the book of Leviticus. In the King James words: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." The next verse gives the reason: so that each generation knows that God made the children of Israel dwell in booths when they came out of Egypt. Second, the roof. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law, works out what makes a booth count. In paraphrase: if the sunlight inside is more than the shade, it isn't a proper sukkah. So the roof has to give real shade, yet stay loose, made of things that grew from the ground. Shelter, but not a fortress. Third, the timing. This is a harvest festival. You'd expect the moment the grain is safely stored to be the moment you settle into your strongest house. Instead, the Torah sends people out under a fragile roof, at the very moment of plenty. Some read it as a reminder that the full barn isn't what keeps you safe. Fourth, the joy. Deuteronomy says of this feast, "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast," and then lists who rejoices: sons and daughters, servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow. The booth isn't for the family alone. It's a table with room for whoever is outside. That makes a fitting end to this week, which looked at listening in meetings, softening messages, leaving work on time, naming a stage of life, play, and thanking the workers. Sukkot adds one more: when the work is done, step out from behind the walls and make room.
screen: `YE SHALL DWELL IN BOOTHS.` · `MORE SHADE THAN SUN.` · `A FRAGILE ROOF AT HARVEST.` · `ROOM FOR THE STRANGER.` · then, large: `SUKKOT.`

segments.voice: If you can, move closer to a window, or step outside for this practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice what's over your head right now: a ceiling, a sky, branches, clouds. Then picture a roof of leaves, with light coming through the gaps. Ask yourself what keeps you safe, really. Then think about one meal this week you could eat outside, under the sky, and who you could invite to share it. If you pray, you can hold that table in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Sukkot. Booths. The Jewish harvest festival when families live in huts open to the sky, with room for the stranger. Today's word.
Your line: the booth. Eat one meal outside this week, under the sky, and leave room at the table for someone. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: During Sukkot, Jewish families build a sukkah, a hut roofed with branches, and eat meals in it, with some sleeping there too; guests are welcomed into the booth.

myth: a sukkah's roof must keep out all light
in the Mishnah, it needs more shade than sun, but it's laid loose, from things that grew.
Leviticus gives the booths a reason: remembering the way out of Egypt
so each generation knows God made Israel dwell in booths.
in Deuteronomy, the feast is for the family alone
the stranger, the fatherless and the widow rejoice too.
